translations.title: And God Made Me a Woman
translations.text:
And God made me a woman,
with long hair,
a woman's eyes, nose, and mouth.

With curves
and folds
and gentle hollows,
God hollowed me out inside,
made me a workshop
for human beings.

God delicately wove my nerves
and carefully balanced
the measure of my hormones.
God made my blood
and filled me with it
so it would flow
throughout my body;
thus were born
ideas,
dreams,
instinct.

God created it all gently,
with hammer blows of breath
and drill strokes of love,
the thousand and one things
that make me a woman every day,
for which I rise with pride
every morning
and bless my sex.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: I Hate Conventional Poetry...
translations.text:
“I hate conventional poetry: it readily
offers its flabby sides to the crowd;
it stretches out in routine embraces,
languid, and sleeps.

I want a living stanza that leaps
with the rhythm of feet and clapping hands in choruses;
I catch its wing in flight, and it, untamed,
resists and struggles.”

Version by Carlos López Narváez
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Someone Is Saved by Hearing the Nightingale
translations.text:
A poem to remember Alice
in the mirror

Here the legendary and the real
Our story resembles

That of the marvelous girl who entered the mirror
She was always on the verge of disappearing

But no one spoke the formula that would return her to dust
Neither Tweedledum nor Tweedledee nor the Queen nor the Red King

Who had only to wake up
Perhaps we are a story

Perhaps without ever realizing it
The ship of Ulysses
Or Keats's nightingale

(That bird not destined for death)
Let us say, then, that what was a canto of the Odyssey

Will continue to be us
While remaining Wonderland

And someone may recognize us
On hearing the story not yet written

In the castle story, the many-mooned story
In the story of a broken toy

The story, at last, of when a cloud passed over Alice
Perhaps we are the shadow of that blue upon her hand

translations.title: The Mother
translations.text:
And when the heart's last beat
has brought down the wall of shadow,
to lead me, mother, to the Lord,
you will give me your hand once more.

On your knees, resolute,
you will be a statue before the Eternal,
as I already saw you
when you were still alive.

Trembling, you will raise your aged arms,
as you did when you breathed your last,
saying: My God, here I am.

And only when he has forgiven me
will you want to look at me.

You will remember waiting so long for me,
and a swift sigh will pass through your eyes.

Version by Jesús López Pacheco

translations.title: The Poet Is Not a Poet
translations.text:
The poet is not a poet
until the people read us.

translations.title: I Dedicated My Book
translations.text:
I dedicated my book to a one-year-old girl,
and she liked it so much
that she ate it.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: The Woman Poet
translations.text:
The woman poet married the man poet,
and instead of having a child,
they had a sonnet.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: On Clear Nights
translations.text:
On clear nights,
I solve the problem of being alone.

I invite the moon, and with my shadow we are three.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.
